claims.text: Adding a small, controlled volume fraction of WS2 as a secondary phase to a high-entropy alloy will reduce its coefficient of friction across a wide service-temperature range.
Adding a small, controlled volume fraction of WS2 as a secondary phase to a high-entropy alloy will reduce its wear rate across a wide service-temperature range.
Uniformly dispersed WS2 nanoparticles will form localized lubricious tribofilms at sliding-contact interfaces.
Incorporating WS2 nanoparticles will not compromise the structural integrity of the high-entropy-alloy matrix.
Mechanical sliding will cause WS2 to initiate formation of a stable, low-shear-strength tribolayer at the wear interface.
The WS2-derived tribofilm will minimize direct metal-to-metal contact.
Minimizing direct metal-to-metal contact through the WS2-derived tribofilm will reduce friction.
Minimizing direct metal-to-metal contact through the WS2-derived tribofilm will reduce wear.
WS2 is sufficiently stable at elevated temperatures for its lubrication effect to persist across a wide temperature range.
The WS2-modified alloy may improve friction coefficient and wear rate by approximately tens of percent relative to the untreated alloy.
The lubrication benefit depends on WS2 remaining well dispersed and stable within the alloy matrix.
Temperatures above the stability limit of WS2 may diminish the tribological benefit.
WS2 particle agglomeration may diminish the tribological benefit.
Reaction between WS2 and the alloy matrix may diminish the tribological benefit.
There is an optimum WS2 volume fraction that balances lubrication performance against retention of mechanical properties.
Failure to obtain statistically significant reductions in both friction coefficient and wear rate across the tested temperature range relative to an unmodified control would falsify the hypothesis.
Compromise of alloy structural integrity following WS2 addition would falsify the hypothesis.
